headline: Trump says his 250-foot arch will hold snipers and drones
summary: President Trump said Sunday that the arch he wants between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery will double as a military complex: drones and snipers on the roof and plaza, ammunition in storage. He says the military asked. The Pentagon said it had nothing beyond his statement. A lawsuit says Congress must approve it.

cover_question.q: Did the military really ask for it?

cover_answer: He says so. The Pentagon says it has nothing to add.
table_question: Should a monument do a second job, or just stand there?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president wants to build a huge arch near Washington, half as tall as the Washington Monument. On Sunday he said soldiers would keep watch from the top. It isn't built yet, and lots of grown-ups still have to say yes. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A tall thing and a job for it. A five-year-old can picture both, and “not built yet” is the reassurance. At this age one vivid detail stands in for the whole story, so the detail is the height, not the snipers.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them a height they can picture, half the Washington Monument, and one plain job for the building. The snipers stay out. Expect “can we go up it?” Not yet: it is a plan, and lots of people still have to agree.

8-12.script: Trump wants a 250-foot arch at the bridge into Washington. On Sunday he said it will hold drones and snipers too, because the military asked. The Pentagon had nothing to add. Think of a permission slip: a commission still has to vote, and a lawsuit says Congress must sign too.
8-12.why: A chain with a gap in it, and a permission slip they have carried.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults apply the rules to themselves, so the script gives them the chain: a plan, a new claim about it, and the signatures it still needs. The permission slip is the mechanism; they have carried one. Expect “can he just do it?” Not on his own. A commission still has to vote.

13-17.script: What do you make of it when the president says the military asked for something and the Pentagon has nothing to add? That's the arch: snipers and drones, he says, at the military's request. If a building is called national security, should it need fewer approvals, or more?
13-17.why: Two claims that don't quite meet. Let them decide what the gap means.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once and reason about what is not in front of them, and this story is that: a claim from the president, silence from the Pentagon, a label now on two buildings. The script hands them the gap, not a verdict. Expect “so is he lying?” Say what is known, then ask what would count as evidence.

5-7.q: Why would an arch have soldiers in it?
5-7.a: He says the army asked for a place to keep watch from. It isn't built yet, and lots of people still have to say yes.

8-12.q: Can he just build whatever he wants?
8-12.a: No. A commission still has to vote, and a lawsuit says Congress must too.
Half the Washington Monument. Two and a half Lincoln Memorials.

13-17.q: Did the military really ask for it?
13-17.a: He says so. The Pentagon said it had nothing beyond his statement.

13-17.q: Why does it matter what he calls it?
13-17.a: He called the ballroom one too. BBC says the approvals are unclear.
